Bishop Hill fully demolished, no protest from neighbourhood

Mr So said he received the demolition notice at the end of July and immediately contacted Sham Shui Po district councillors, hoping to preserve the fitness equipment on Wozi Mountain, but was told in response that "none of the equipment would be retained." Mr So said that in previous demolitions, residents had managed to organise petitions and protests, but this time the notice period was too short to mobilise the community. As a result, the morning exercise spot residents had enjoyed for over 20 years will come to an end.

Three days ago (the 10th), the Home Affairs Department announced the Wozi Mountain improvement plan, stating that the government would remove illegal and unsafe structures, facilities and杂物 on the hill in phases, noting that these items had long been illegally occupying government land.

Yesterday (the 12th), at around 6:30 a.m., staff from the Lands Department and uniformed police arrived, cordoning off the Tongyin Street hillside sitting-out area from base to summit. Workers immediately moved in to carry away fitness equipment, bicycles, ping-pong tables and other items. Police deployed冲锋车 and prisoner transport vans as a precaution. Mr So said this is merely a place where residents exercise, and he could not understand the purpose of the police presence: "The officers just stood there, watching us the whole time. What have we done? Are we rioters? Have we broken the law?"

"Morning exercise haven" becomes LCSD facility

Mr So said residents crowdfunded a total of HK$400,000 to build the Bishop Hill "morning exercise haven," which included a ping-pong table, fitness equipment, and unofficial hiking trails built decades ago. On demolition day, many residents were still doing morning exercises and using the equipment. Several residents said they felt deep sorrow at losing the place they had exercised in for years. Some kept asking Mr So what to do, but he himself did not know.

He said he had spent several consecutive days dismantling the fitness equipment, hoping to preserve as much of his own handiwork as possible. He has now removed all the muscle massage rollers, while some residents wish to relocate certain statues to Lantau Island.

According to the Home Affairs Department's Wozi Mountain improvement plan, the "morning exercise haven" will be turned into an LCSD facility; the homemade fitness equipment on the hill will be replaced with standard LCSD recreational equipment; and religious leaders will be invited to properly handle the statues.

Cheated death, built Bishop Hill "morning exercise haven"

75-year-old So Chi-keung is a SARS survivor. Due to side effects from medication, he suffered后遗症 including muscle pain, weakness and fatigue. After three years of physiotherapy, his condition showed no improvement. In 2008, at a neighbour's invitation, So went to Bishop Hill for morning exercise and found his spirits lifted, which he attributed to the fresh mountain air. He then began exercising at Bishop Hill every morning at six. After persisting for a month, he regained his health and strength, and decided to stop physiotherapy altogether.

In 2009, Mr So travelled to Korea and was inspired by the local fitness facilities. After returning to Hong Kong, he used his own hardware factory to "homemade-style" produce a bicycle machine and a cable machine, then carried the disassembled parts up Bishop Hill by himself. He described the manufacturing as simple, but transporting the equipment up the mountain was extremely difficult. Over four years, he built more than 20 pieces of fitness equipment on Bishop Hill, including swings, balance bars and rollers, placing them on the open space above the current Sham Shui Po service reservoir. Initially, some elderly residents opposed him, but after using the equipment, neighbours found relief from physical ailments, and the facilities became hugely popular.

Bishop Hill exposed for the first time, residents protest demolition

Mr So said that in 2014, over 200 young people held a psychedelic party on Bishop Hill, creating a noise nuisance. When police arrived, they discovered for the first time a large number of privately built fitness installations. The Water Supplies Department subsequently increased patrols of Bishop Hill and repeatedly drove away residents exercising there, and planned to demolish the facilities. At that time, Mr So organised several protest activities and personally went to the Sham Shui Po District Council Secretariat to fight for the retention of the fitness ground.

Accidental check-in: Bishop Hill reservoir becomes Grade 1 historic building

In 2017, the Water Supplies Department planned to clear the unauthorised structures on Bishop Hill and return the land to the Lands Department. Additionally, the roots of two large trees on top of the reservoir had extended into the structure, posing a collapse risk. In 2020, as preparations began for tree removal and reservoir backfilling, the Water Supplies Department promised Mr So that his fitness equipment could be placed on the filled land, and So agreed to the works.

As a result, on Christmas Eve, Mr So and a volunteer sneaked into the reservoir to check if anything had been left behind, and posted photos on social media. The post attracted large crowds to check in at the reservoir, drawing public attention. Mr So said the public protested against the demolition because of the reservoir's historical value. One regular Bishop Hill user, Auntie Fong, even stood in front of an excavator to stop the demolition work.

In 2021, the reservoir was graded as a Grade 1 historic building by the Antiquities Advisory Committee. The reservoir was preserved and opened to the public, and Mr So relocated his fitness equipment to the foot of the hill.

Mao Zedong statue incident may have triggered demolition

In June 2022, the Sham Shui Po District Management Committee wanted to remove the shrines and fitness facilities. Mr So launched a petition to fight for retention, stating that a total of 3,399 Sham Shui Po district residents had signed, and he delivered the letter to the Home Affairs Department, pledging not to expand the facilities further.

Mr So said that after this, Bishop Hill remained stable, and the government did not indicate that a full clearance was necessary. However, in early 2026, resident Auntie Fong set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop Hill. Although these were later removed, Mr So believes the Mao Zedong incident reignited government attention to Bishop Hill. Coupled with some residents making loud noise on the hill and disturbing nearby residents, the government decided to fully demolish the site.

In early 2026, resident Auntie Fong set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop Hill, reigniting controversy over the use of the site. (File photo)

"Without Bishop Hill, I would have lived 20 years less"

Watching workers dismantle the fitness equipment he had built piece by piece, Mr So did not show grief. He plans to take the equipment he himself has dismantled back to his ancestral home, and he continues to tell the media about Bishop Hill's history. In fact, he is well aware that the "morning exercise haven" has been in violation of regulations for years, but he believes the place has benefited many residents. He hopes that by telling Bishop Hill's story, he can gain government recognition. Although retention was ultimately not granted, he still wants to pass the story on, to repay Bishop Hill for what it has given him.

He bade farewell to Bishop Hill: "I'm grateful it gave me a new life. Without it, I'd be 20 years shorter—I should be dead. Without Bishop Hill, I'd be dead... And I'm a SARS survivor who's been through so much. Do you think I could have lived until today?"
